passages.t: A man with dropsy, on the Sabbath
passages.happening:
One Sabbath Jesus goes to eat “in the home of a leading Pharisee, and those in attendance were watching Him closely” (verse 1).

Right in front of him is a man with dropsy. Jesus asks the experts in the law and the Pharisees, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?” (verse 3). They say nothing.

So Jesus takes hold of the man, heals him, and sends him on his way. Then he asks them, “Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?” (verse 5). Again, they cannot answer.
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this healing.

Dropsy is an old name for a swelling of the body, when fluid gathers under the skin, often in the legs or the belly. Today it is usually a sign of a deeper illness. Ancient doctors held that people with dropsy were always thirsty, and that drinking only made the swelling worse. So Greek and Roman writers used dropsy as a picture of greed: the more you get, the more you want. The Roman poet Horace used it that way in one of his odes. Some scholars think Luke's first readers would have heard this healing as an opening to the whole chapter, which is about the hunger for honour and for money. Luke does not say so, and the man himself was simply ill.

This is the third time in Luke that Jesus eats in a Pharisee's home (7:36; 11:37). It is also the third time that a healing on the Sabbath stirs up an objection (6:6-11; 13:10-17). The Pharisees were devout Jews who tried to keep God's law in the whole of ordinary life (see the note on 11:37-44). The Sabbath, the seventh day, was a gift from God and a sign of his covenant with Israel, and no work was to be done on it. These men are not villains for caring about it.

‘Watching Him closely’ means they were watching to see what he would do. This time Jesus speaks first. He asks his question before he heals, so that everyone in the room has to decide what they think. Their silence says a great deal. In a world where honour was won or lost in public, being unable to answer a question at a host's table was a defeat that everyone could see.

Jesus' second question comes from the farm and the home. If your own child, or even your ox, fell into a pit or a well on the Sabbath, you would pull them out at once. No one in the room would wait until the day was over. Then why should this man wait?
passages.ot: The Sabbath law itself was full of mercy. Rest was given to the whole household, slaves and animals included, “so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do” (Deuteronomy 5:14). And Israel was told why: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (Deuteronomy 5:15). The Sabbath was a day of freedom. Jesus treats healing as exactly the kind of thing the day was for.
passages.hard: Did Jesus break the Sabbath? He never says the Sabbath does not matter. He asks what the Sabbath is for. The law he answers to is God's own law, and he reads it as a law of mercy. His hearers already lived that way with their own families and animals. He only asks them to show a sick stranger the same mercy.
passages.asks: The man with dropsy never speaks. He was simply there, and Jesus took hold of him. Ask who is ‘right there before’ you, the person everyone in the room has learned not to see. And ask whether your rules, even good ones, have ever become a reason to make someone else wait for help.

passages.happening:
Jesus notices how the guests are choosing the places of honour at the table, and he tells them a parable.

When you are invited to a wedding banquet, he says, do not sit in the place of honour. Someone more important may come, and the host will say, ‘Give this man your seat.’ Then, “in humiliation, you will have to take the last place” (verse 9).

Instead, go and sit in the last place. Then the host may come and say, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ “Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you” (verse 10).

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
At a formal dinner in Jesus' world, guests lay on couches around low tables, leaning on one elbow. The places nearest the host were the places of honour. Where you lay told everyone in the room what you were worth.

In that world, honour was a public verdict. It was not mainly what you thought of yourself. It was what the people around you said you were worth, out loud and in front of others. To be moved down the table, with everyone watching, was real shame. The site's portrait of honour and shame in the Bible's world shows how much depended on it, and notes that Jesus' advice here says almost word for word what Proverbs had already said.

Luke calls this advice a parable. That is a clue. Jesus is not only giving lessons in good manners. The dinner is a picture of standing before God. The last line says so: it is God who humbles and God who lifts up.
passages.ot:
Proverbs gave the same advice long before: “Do not exalt yourself in the presence of the king, and do not stand in the place of great men; for it is better that he says to you, ‘Come up here!’ than that you should be demoted in the presence of the prince” (Proverbs 25:6-7).

And Hannah sang of the God who reverses places: “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor” (1 Samuel 2:8). Mary sings the same song in Luke: “He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52).
passages.hard:
Is Jesus teaching a clever way to get honour in the end? Take the low seat, and you will be called up higher. Some have read it that way. But that would only be a quieter way of grasping for status. The point of the parable is that honour is God's to give. The humble person is not playing a longer game. They have stopped keeping score.

Does humility mean thinking you are worthless? No. The person in the last seat is still an invited guest, and the host calls them ‘Friend’. Humility in the Bible is not hating yourself. It is trusting God with your worth, so that you no longer need to win it at the table.
passages.asks: Where do you reach for the best seat: in a meeting, a conversation, online, even in church? Ask what it would look like to let God decide your place this week. And notice the word the host uses for the one in the last seat: ‘Friend’.

passages.happening:
Then Jesus turns to the man who invited him. “When you host a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors. Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid” (verse 12).

“But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Among people with money, invitations were a kind of trade. I invite you, you invite me, and both of us gain honour from being seen together. Everyone knew the rules. A good guest list was a way of climbing.

Jesus tells his host to break the circle. Invite the people who can never invite you back. The poor had nothing to give. People who were disabled often had no work and lived by begging. They could add nothing to a host's name. That is exactly why Jesus names them.

His list is pointed. Some Jewish groups of the time drew sharp lines around who could belong. One of the Dead Sea Scrolls, a rule for the gathering of God's people at the end of the age (often called the Rule of the Congregation), shuts out the lame, the blind, the deaf and others with a visible defect, because holy angels would be present. Jesus' list sounds almost like the opposite. The people others left out are the first ones he says to invite.

Jesus does not say there is no reward. He says the reward comes from God, ‘at the resurrection of the righteous’, not from the guests.
passages.ot:
The Law had already set a table for those with nothing. Every three years a tenth of the harvest was stored up so that “the Levite (because he has no portion or inheritance among you), the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow within your gates may come and eat and be satisfied” (Deuteronomy 14:29).

The priests' law in Leviticus kept a man who was “blind, lame, disfigured, or deformed” from offering the sacrifices (Leviticus 21:18). Yet King David brought Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, to his own table: “he always ate at the king’s table, and he was lame in both feet” (2 Samuel 9:13). And Proverbs says, “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender” (Proverbs 19:17).
passages.hard:
Is this only a way of speaking, or does Jesus mean real meals? Some readers turn it into a general call to a generous heart. Luke means more than that. He shows the first Christians sharing their tables and their goods with anyone in need (Acts 2:44-46). Jesus means real food and real guests.

That does not mean it is wrong to eat with friends and family. Jesus himself ate with friends. It means a table that only ever holds people who can pay us back is too small.
passages.asks: Look at the last few people you have had to your table, or out for a meal. Could any of them not repay you? Ask who in your town, or your church, is never invited anywhere. Jesus does not ask you to feel generous. He asks you to send an invitation.

passages.t: The great banquet, and ‘compel them to come in’
passages.happening:
One of the guests hears Jesus speak of the resurrection and says, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God” (verse 15).

Jesus answers with a story. A man prepares a great banquet and invites many guests. When the meal is ready he sends his servant to tell them, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ But they all begin to make excuses. One has bought a field and must go and see it. Another has bought five pairs of oxen and is going to try them out. A third has just married and cannot come.

The master is angry. He tells his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame’ (verse 21). The servant does it, and there is still room. So the master says, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, so that my house will be full’ (verse 23).

“For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The guest's remark sounds pious. Many Jews pictured the age to come as a great feast with God, and he assumes that he and the people around him will be there. Jesus' story answers him: the people who expect a seat may turn it down, and the people who never expected one will fill the house.

The story assumes two calls. First the guests were invited, and they accepted. Then, when the food was ready, a servant came to fetch them. The book of Esther shows something like it, when the king's servants come to rush Haman to Esther's banquet (Esther 6:14). So these guests had already said yes. To say no at the last moment, after the meat was cooked, was a public insult to the host.

Look at the excuses. A field does not go anywhere; it could be seen tomorrow. Oxen could be tried another day. The third man does not even ask to be excused. The Law did let a newly married man stay home for a year, but that was from war, not from a dinner he had promised to come to (Deuteronomy 24:5). The excuses are polite, and they are empty. The guests simply prefer something else.

Then the house fills. First with the poor and disabled of the town, the very list from verse 13. Then with people from the roads and the hedges outside the town: travellers, labourers, people with no home in that place. Many readers have seen in them the people of every nation, to whom the good news goes in Luke's second book, Acts.

Matthew tells a similar story in a different form (Matthew 22:1-14). There a king gives a wedding feast for his son. The guests not only refuse but kill his servants, and the king sends troops and burns their city. Luke's story is quieter and closer to an ordinary dinner. Some scholars think Jesus told the story more than once, in different ways; others think the two Gospels shaped one story for their readers. Either way, both end with a full house of unexpected guests.
passages.ot:
The prophets pictured God's feast: “On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat, of finely aged wine” (Isaiah 25:6). It is for ‘all the peoples’, and in the next lines God “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8).

And Isaiah gives the invitation: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1). The guests in Jesus' story pay nothing. They only have to come.
passages.hard:
‘Compel them to come in’ (verse 23). These words have a dark history, and it must be told plainly. Augustine, the great North African bishop, at first held that no one should be forced into the church. Around AD 408, in a letter to Vincentius, a bishop of the Donatists, a church that had broken away from the main church in North Africa, he wrote that he had changed his mind, and he pointed to this verse to defend using the laws of the Roman empire to press the Donatists back into the church. Later churches went much further. For centuries ‘compel them to come in’ was quoted to justify forcing people into the church, by law, by punishment, and by violence. In 1686 a French Protestant refugee named Pierre Bayle wrote a whole book on this one verse, as Protestants in France were being forced to become Catholic. He argued that forcing anyone to act against their own conscience is a deep wrong, and that any reading of Scripture that leads to such cruelty must be false.

That reading is wrong, and this site rejects it. The verse does not give anyone, church or state, the right to force faith on a single person.

Look at the story itself. The host has no soldiers. He has one servant, and the servant has nothing but an invitation. The people on the roads outside town would never believe that a rich man's feast was meant for them. They would hang back, as poor people do when they are asked into a grand house. So the servant has to insist, to urge, to keep on asking until they believe it. The host is pleading, not coercing. The Greek verb can mean to force, but it can also mean to urge strongly. Mark uses it when Jesus ‘made’ his disciples get into the boat (Mark 6:45). Luke uses a similar strong word for the two disciples at Emmaus, who “pleaded with Him” to stay (Luke 24:29). And Jesus himself never forced anyone. When two of his disciples wanted to call down fire on a village that would not receive him, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55).

The Catholic Church taught at the Second Vatican Council, in 1965, that no one is to be forced to act against their conscience in matters of religion, and Baptists and many other Christians have long said the same. Faith that is forced is not faith. The only compelling the gospel knows is the compelling of love: “We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

If you were once pushed, shamed or pressured into a religious decision, that was not the way of Jesus. His invitation still stands, and it is still an invitation. You are free to come, and free to take your time.

Is the master's anger in verse 21, and the closing verdict in verse 24, a threat? It is the sorrow and anger of a host whose open table was refused. Those who were shut out shut themselves out. No one in the story is kept away who wanted to come.
passages.asks: The guests did not hate the host. They had fields and oxen and a new home, all good things, and they preferred them. Ask what good things in your life have become your polite excuse. And then ask the other question: do you believe the invitation is really meant for you, even if you feel like someone from the hedges? The servant was sent to keep asking until people believed it.

passages.t: Hate father and mother? Counting the cost
passages.happening:
Large crowds are now travelling with Jesus. He turns and says to them that anyone who comes to him and “does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters” and even his own life “cannot be My disciple” (verse 26). “And whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple” (verse 27).

Then he tells two short parables. Who would start to build a tower without first sitting down to count the cost? If he lays the foundation and cannot finish, everyone who sees it will laugh: ‘This man could not finish what he started to build’ (verse 30). And what king goes to war against another king without first sitting down to ask whether his ten thousand men can face twenty thousand? If not, he sends messengers while the other army is still far off, to ask for terms of peace.

“In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The crowds are large, and Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem (9:51). Many were following because of the healings and the meals. Jesus turns round to tell them where the road leads.

‘Hate’ is the word that stops every reader. In the Hebrew way of speaking, ‘hate’ can mean ‘love less’ when two loves are compared. Genesis says Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah”, and the next verse, in Hebrew, says Leah was ‘hated’, which the BSB rightly translates as “unloved” (Genesis 29:30-31). Matthew's version of this saying puts it plainly: anyone who loves father or mother more than Jesus is not worthy of him (Matthew 10:37). Luke keeps the sharper word. Some readers think it was chosen because a comparison alone is too gentle; either way, the point is first place. Luke's list also includes ‘wife’, as his list of what disciples have left behind does later (18:29), and it ends with ‘even his own life’. The point is not anger at other people. It is that nothing, not even your own life, comes before Jesus.

In the ancient world, family was everything. It gave you your name, your work, your land, your place in the village and your care in old age. Following Jesus could cost all of that. Some of his first followers were cut off by their own families, as he warned (12:51-53).

A cross was not a picture of ordinary troubles. A man carrying a cross was a condemned man walking to his death. Luke has already told of Jesus' call to ‘take up his cross daily’ (see the note on 9:23-27).

The two parables have the same shape. A builder with a half-finished tower became a joke, and the unfinished stones would stand there for everyone to see. A king who marched out without counting his soldiers could lose his army and his throne. Wars between small kings were real in Jesus' day: around AD 36 Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, lost his army to Aretas, king of the Nabataeans, as the historian Josephus tells.

Then the last line: ‘give up everything he has’. Peter, James and John ‘left everything’ when they followed (5:11), and so did Levi (5:28).
passages.ot:
The Law placed honour to parents right after the commands about God: “Honor your father and mother” (Exodus 20:12). Jesus himself kept that law, and he condemned those who used religion to dodge caring for their parents (Mark 7:9-13). So when he asks for a love that comes before father and mother, he is claiming a place that, in Israel's Scriptures, belongs to God alone.

And there is comfort for those whose families turn away: “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10).
passages.hard:
Does Jesus tell his followers to despise their families? No. He asks for first place, not for cruelty. The same Jesus repeats the command, ‘honor your father and mother’ (18:20). From the cross he made sure his own mother would be cared for (John 19:26-27). And the New Testament says plainly, “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). Groups that have used this verse to cut people off from their parents, husbands, wives or children have read it wrongly. The division Jesus speaks of comes from others' response to him, not from his followers' hostility.

But the word should not be softened into nothing either. For many believers in the world today, as in the first century, following Jesus means being disowned. Jesus wants no one to follow him without knowing it might cost that much.

If your family has rejected you for your faith, you are not alone, and you have not failed. The psalmist wrote, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). Jesus promised that no one who has left home or family for his sake will lose out (Mark 10:29-30). Keep loving them, keep the door open as far as you safely can, and find a church family who will stand with you. If rejection has turned into threats or harm, seeking safety is not disloyalty to Jesus. Please speak to someone you trust, and if you are in danger, contact the police or a crisis line.

Must every Christian sell everything? Christians have read verse 33 in two ways, as they read Jesus' words to the rich man (see the note on 18:18-30). Some have taken them literally and given all they owned away. Many hold that Jesus asks every disciple to hand everything over to him, so that nothing they own is really theirs any more, while some are called to give it all away. In Acts, believers sold land to help the poor, yet Peter tells Ananias that his land was his own to keep or sell (Acts 5:4). Either way, verse 33 does not let anyone keep a corner of life that Jesus may not touch.

Does counting the cost mean waiting until you are sure you can pay? No. No one could pay this cost in their own strength. The parables warn against a careless following that has never thought about the cross. They are not a reason to stay away until you feel ready.
passages.asks: Jesus does not hide the price. Ask what you have quietly kept out of his reach: a person, a plan, your money, your own life. And ask whether you have ever stopped to count the cost of following him, or only the cost of not following.

passages.happening:
Jesus ends with a short picture. “Salt is good, but if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned?” (verse 34). It is no use for the soil or even for the manure heap. It is thrown out.

“He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew have this saying too, in other places (Mark 9:49-50; Matthew 5:13). Salt was one of the most ordinary things in an ancient kitchen. It flavoured food and kept meat and fish from going bad. How salt could lose its taste has been explained in different ways, and no one explanation is agreed. The picture is plain enough: salt that does not do what salt does is useless.

Luke adds something the others do not: salt without its taste is no good even for the soil or the manure pile. It is simply thrown away. And Luke places the saying right after the cost of following Jesus. A disciple who will not pay that cost is like salt with no taste.

‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear’ is the same call that ended the story of the sower (8:8). Jesus wants the crowd to stop and listen, not just to keep walking with him.
passages.ot: In Israel's worship every grain offering had to be seasoned with salt, “the salt of the covenant of your God” (Leviticus 2:13). Salt stood for a covenant that lasts.
passages.asks: Salt is meant to be different from what it touches. Ask whether your following of Jesus still makes any difference to the people and places around you, or whether it has lost its taste. Then listen, as he asked.
